reference.source: Mandell, Douglas and Bennett / ATS-IDSA NTM guidance
clinicalPearls: A rapidly growing mycobacterium found in soil and water that most often causes localised skin, soft-tissue, and wound infection
Classically causes post-surgical wound infection, including sternal wounds after cardiac surgery and infection after breast augmentation, and catheter-related infection
A well-recognised cause of furunculosis of the lower legs and feet after nail-salon footbaths (pedicure-associated furunculosis)
Pulmonary disease is uncommon and, when it occurs, is often linked to oesophageal disorders and chronic aspiration
Although a macrolide may appear active in vitro, a functional inducible macrolide-resistance gene can emerge, so this should be tested for
Often susceptible to a broader range of oral agents than M. abscessus, including fluoroquinolones, tetracyclines, and sulfonamides, giving more treatment options
Management is with susceptibility-guided combination therapy together with surgical debridement and removal of infected foreign material
reference.pathophysiology: Mycobacterium fortuitum is a ubiquitous rapidly growing mycobacterium of soil and water. Most infections follow inoculation through trauma, surgery, injection, catheters, or contaminated water, producing localised abscesses, wound infection, or furuncles; outbreaks have been traced to footbaths in nail salons. Pulmonary infection is unusual and is associated with conditions predisposing to aspiration, such as achalasia and gastro-oesophageal reflux. Although generally less virulent and more antibiotic-susceptible than M. abscessus, the organism can carry an inducible macrolide-resistance mechanism, and retained foreign material or undrained collections allow persistent infection.
additionalDifferentials: Other rapidly growing mycobacteria (M. abscessus, M. chelonae)
Ordinary bacterial wound infection or abscess
additionalInvestigations: Culture of wound, tissue, or sputum showing rapid mycobacterial growth
Drug-susceptibility testing including detection of inducible macrolide resistance
Imaging of the surgical site or affected area to define collections
Investigation for an oesophageal or aspiration disorder in pulmonary disease
Review for a common environmental or procedural source in clustered cases
redFlags: Sternal wound or mediastinal infection after cardiac surgery
Prosthesis- or catheter-related infection requiring device removal
Clustered post-procedural cases suggesting a contaminated source
Pulmonary disease with an underlying oesophageal or aspiration disorder
reference.prognosis: Localised skin and wound infection generally has a good prognosis with combined antimicrobial and surgical treatment, aided by the organism's relatively broad susceptibility. Deep surgical-site, prosthesis-related, and pulmonary infections are more difficult and depend on adequate source control and management of predisposing conditions.
pitfalls: Relying on apparent in vitro macrolide activity without testing for inducible resistance
Failing to achieve source control by removing infected material or draining collections
Overlooking an oesophageal or aspiration disorder in pulmonary cases
Missing a shared footbath or injection source in clustered furunculosis
references: Mandell, Douglas, and Bennett's Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases
ATS/IDSA guideline on nontuberculous mycobacterial diseases
management: Exploit its relatively broad susceptibility with a susceptibility-guided oral combination drawn from fluoroquinolones, tetracyclines such as doxycycline or minocycline, and sulfonamides such as co-trimoxazole
Test specifically for inducible macrolide resistance before relying on a macrolide, since a functional resistance gene can emerge despite apparent in vitro activity
Achieve source control by debriding or draining infected surgical sites and removing infected catheters or prosthetic material such as breast implants
Investigate and manage an underlying oesophageal or aspiration disorder where pulmonary disease is present
Monitor treatment response and drug toxicity across the prolonged course, imaging affected sites to define collections
Investigate a common environmental or procedural source, such as nail-salon footbaths, in clustered cases
Refer to infectious diseases, recognising that deep, prosthesis-related, and pulmonary disease depend heavily on adequate source control
